q: The flow of electrons from a place of lower potential to a place of higher potential is called an electric current.
e: True. The flow of electrons from a place of lower potential to a place of higher potential is called an electric current. Electron flow is from low potential to high potential. That flow of charge is an electric current.

q: The flow of electrons from a place of higher potential to a place of lower potential is called an electric current.
e: False. The claim puts higher where lower belongs. The flow of electrons from a place of lower potential to a place of higher potential is called an electric current. Electrons are negative, so they drift from lower potential toward higher potential.

q: In general, an electric current is a flow of electric charge from one place to another.
e: True. In general, an electric current is a flow of electric charge from one place to another. Coulomb's law is K Q1 Q2 / r² along the line joining the charges.

q: The amount of charge passing through a cross-sectional area of a conductor in one second is called an electric current.
e: True. The amount of charge passing through a cross-sectional area of a conductor in one second is called an electric current. Electric current is charge passing a cross-section per second, I = Q/t.

q: The rate of flow of electric charge through a cross-sectional area of a conductor is called an electric current.
e: True. The rate of flow of electric charge through a cross-sectional area of a conductor is called an electric current. Electric current is charge passing a cross-section per second, I = Q/t.
False. Current is treated as a scalar in this definition: charge per unit time through a face.

q: Suppose that the amount of charge $Q$ passes through a cross-sectional area of a conductor in time $t$, the current $I$ flowing through the conductor is $I = \frac{Q}{t}$.
e: True. Suppose that the amount of charge Q passes through a cross-sectional area of a conductor in time t, the current I flowing through the conductor is I = (Q)/(t). The defining equation is I = Q/t.

q: If the number of electrons passing through a cross-sectional area of a conductor is $n$, the amount of charge $Q$ is $Q = ne$.
e: True. If the number of electrons passing through a cross-sectional area of a conductor is n, the amount of charge Q is Q = ne. If n electrons pass, Q = ne, with e the elementary charge.

q: In the SI system, the unit of electric current is ampere (A) in honour of the French physicist, Andre Ampere.
e: True. In the SI system, the unit of electric current is ampere (A) in honour of the French physicist, Andre Ampere. Current is charge per second. Conventional current is opposite to electron drift.

q: 1 A is equivalent to 1 C s.
e: False. 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹, 1 mA = 10⁻³ A, and 1 μA = 10⁻⁶ A.
True. 1 milliampere (mA) is equal to 10^-3 A. 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹, 1 mA = 10⁻³ A, and 1 μA = 10⁻⁶ A.
True. 1 microampere (μA) is equal to 10^-6 A. 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹, 1 mA = 10⁻³ A, and 1 μA = 10⁻⁶ A.

q: The direction of current is conventionally defined as the direction of the flow of positive charge from a higher potential to a lower potential.
e: True. The direction of current is conventionally defined as the direction of the flow of positive charge from a higher potential to a lower potential. Conventional current follows positive charge from high potential to low. Electron flow is the opposite arrow.

q: The direction of current is the same as that of the flow of electrons.
e: False. Conventional current follows positive charge from high potential to low. Electron flow is the opposite arrow.

q: When an electric current is passed through substances, it can produce three main effects: heating effect, chemical effect, and magnetic effect.
e: True. When an electric current is passed through substances, it can produce three main effects: heating effect, chemical effect, and magnetic effect. Current can heat a wire, drive electrolysis, or magnetize a core. Those three effects are used in lamps, plating, and electromagnets.

q: As an electric current flows through the tungsten wire in a bulb, it becomes hot and emits light, demonstrating the heating effect of current.
e: True. As an electric current flows through the tungsten wire in a bulb, it becomes hot and emits light, demonstrating the heating effect of current. Current can heat a wire, drive electrolysis, or magnetize a core. Those three effects are used in lamps, plating, and electromagnets.

q: In the chemical effect of current, copper is deposited on the anode when a current is passed through copper sulphate solution.

q: The chemical effect of current is used in charging batteries, purifying metals, and electro-plating.

q: When a current flows through a coil of insulated wire wound round a bar of soft iron, the bar becomes a magnet and attracts steel pins.
e: True. When a current flows through a coil of insulated wire wound round a bar of soft iron, the bar becomes a magnet and attracts steel pins. A current makes a magnetic field. Soft iron in a solenoid is a temporary magnet; reverse the current and the poles flip.
